C004.subject: GDP per capita
C004.object: material living standards in high-income countries than the Gini coefficient
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in high-income countries than the Gini coefficient]

[PATH:empirical] Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) Database: cross-national panel data on income inequality (Gini coefficients) and material deprivation indicators for high-income countries, 1990-2020 — Directly tests the predictive power of the Gini coefficient versus GDP per capita on material living standards (e.g., housing quality, health outcomes, access to goods) using within-country and between-country variation.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) and OECD Better Life Index: time-series data on GDP per capita and composite well-being measures (e.g., self-reported life satisfaction, material deprivation rates) — Allows comparison of the explanatory power of GDP per capita relative to the Gini coefficient in regression models predicting material living standards, controlling for confounders.

[PATH:literature] Review of theoretical and empirical literature on the 'Easterlin Paradox' and inequality-growth-wellbeing nexus (e.g., Wilkinson & Pickett, 'The Spirit Level'; Kahneman & Deaton, 2010) — Provides synthesized evidence on whether income inequality (Gini) dominates absolute income (GDP per capita) in explaining material and subjective well-being in affluent societies, offering theoretical mechanisms and counterarguments.

C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards in high-income countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in high-income countries]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index (BLI) data, 1990-2020, comparing GDP per capita with multidimensional well-being indicators (housing, income, jobs, community, education, environment, civic engagement, health, life satisfaction, safety, work-life balance) — Directly tests whether GDP per capita correlates with a composite measure of material living standards, revealing discrepancies in high-income countries where non-market factors (e.g., inequality, public services, environmental quality) matter more.

[PATH:empirical] Piketty, Saez, and Zucman (2018) 'Distributional National Accounts' for high-income countries, providing pre- and post-tax income shares and wealth concentration alongside GDP per capita — Examines how median material living standards diverge from GDP per capita when income distribution is unequal, a key critique of GDP as a welfare measure in affluent economies.

[PATH:literature] Stiglitz, Sen, and Fitoussi (2009) 'Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress' (CMEPSP) — Provides a theoretical and empirical framework critiquing GDP as a proxy for well-being, with specific recommendations for alternative metrics (e.g., household income, consumption, wealth) that are more relevant for high-income contexts.

C006.subject: GDP growth
C006.object: subjective wellbeing in low- and middle-income countries after controlling for environmental degradation costs
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth subjective wellbeing in low- and middle-income countries after controlling for environmental degradation costs]

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey longitudinal data merged with World Bank GDP growth statistics and Environmental Performance Index (EPI) for low- and middle-income countries (1990-2020) — Provides direct cross-national time-series data on subjective wellbeing, GDP growth, and environmental degradation costs, enabling a multivariate regression that isolates the hypothesized inverse correlation.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of 'Easterlin Paradox' literature focusing on developing nations, especially studies that incorporate environmental degradation as a control variable — Synthesizes existing findings on the GDP-wellbeing relationship in low- and middle-income contexts, highlighting whether the inverse correlation emerges once environmental costs are accounted for, and identifies gaps in current evidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model from ecological economics linking material throughput (GDP growth) to welfare losses via ecosystem service depletion, applied to developing country data — Provides a causal framework explaining why GDP growth might reduce subjective wellbeing after controlling for environmental degradation, and generates testable predictions for empirical validation.

C007.subject: GDP growth
C007.object: overall economic progress and potential for improving wellbeing
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth overall economic progress and potential for improving wellbeing]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) and Gallup World Poll data (1980-2020) — Cross-country panel data comparing GDP growth rates with multidimensional wellbeing measures (e.g., life satisfaction, health, education, inequality-adjusted income) can test whether GDP growth reliably predicts improvements in wellbeing in low- and middle-income countries over the specified period.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of literature on 'Beyond GDP' indicators (e.g., OECD Better Life Index, UN Human Development Index, Genuine Progress Indicator) — Reviewing meta-analyses and empirical studies that assess correlations between GDP growth and alternative progress metrics can clarify under what conditions GDP growth aligns or diverges from actual wellbeing outcomes, especially in developing economies.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework: Easterlin Paradox and capability approach (e.g., Amartya Sen, Richard Easterlin, Daniel Kahneman) — Engaging with foundational theories that question the linear relationship between income growth and subjective wellbeing or human capabilities provides a conceptual basis for refuting the hypothesis, particularly in contexts where inequality or non-material factors dominate.
